title: Design exercise: vector search service
summary: Design a tenant-isolated vector search service with measured filtered recall, immutable serving segments and an explicit recovery protocol. Distinguish raw vector bytes, graph memory and PQ codes; benchmark serving capacity, publish builds at revision watermarks, and compare a bespoke AWS fleet with managed vector stores.

exercise.prompt: Design a vector search service used by several internal products: callers insert vectors with metadata and query for the nearest neighbours of a query vector, filtered by metadata, with a recall they can rely on and a latency budget they can plan around. The service must keep working while indexes are rebuilt and must not let one product's collection crowd out another.

constraints.caption: Exercise assumptions and targets; not measured production values.
rows: Upsert and delete vectors with a metadata payload; query the k nearest by cosine or dot product with metadata filters; collections per tenant with independent dimensions and distance; a stated recall target per collection; freshness of inserts within one minute; rebuild an index without downtime.
100 million vectors across 50 collections; largest collection 40 million; 768 dimensions.
2,000 peak queries/second; k from 10 to 100; 1 million upserts/day.
100,000 deletes/day; tenant, document id and date-range filters.
Recall at 10 of at least 0.95 against exact search on the collection's own sample set; p99 under 50 ms for unfiltered queries and under 100 ms for filtered ones.
99.9 percent availability for queries; a collection's rebuild never affects another collection's latency.
Computing embeddings (callers bring vectors), text search and hybrid ranking (the RAG exercise), the model that chooses dimensions, analytics over vectors.

clarifying_questions.a: Approximate, with a measured recall against exact search; callers choose a recall tier per query (fast or thorough) that maps to the index's search-time parameter.
Mostly broad (a tenant, a date range covering a large share), sometimes very selective (one document id). Both must work; the strategy differs.

clarifying_questions.q: Can vectors be updated in place?
clarifying_questions.a: This service treats upserts as new caller versions and suppresses old versions with tombstones. Immutable segments are a design choice; not every HNSW implementation forbids updates. FAISS HNSW does not support removal.
The old segments keep serving; the new ones are built beside them and swapped in when their recall check passes.

clarifying_questions.q: Who defines the recall test set?
clarifying_questions.a: Collection owners supply representative query vectors and filters with exact-search ground truth. Every candidate serving generation and parameter change is tested end to end, not only segment by segment.

Often for small collections: pgvector supports HNSW and IVFFlat, with HNSW vector indexes up to 2,000 dimensions and halfvec up to 4,000. Filter selectivity and actual latency must be measured; iterative scans can improve filtered result coverage.

blocks.text: Neither the distance-computation count nor an SSD sequential-bandwidth table proves query capacity. Benchmark actual vector distributions, filters, search parameters, random reads and concurrent builds. A query targets its collection’s shards, not every shard in the service; replicas split normal requests, while hedges add load.

Separate building from serving, but give both a recoverable source of truth. The original independent raw write and log append could lose index updates; here they commit together. Notifications only wake workers. Each replica reconstructs from a pinned segment manifest and retained mutation revisions, so consuming a queue message never destroys another replica’s recovery history.

blocks.caption: API with explicit freshness and idempotency.
rows: accepted (collection_id, shard_id, revision) token per item
Batch reports per-item results; retry only failed items; no implied batch atomicity.
vector, k, filter, recall tier, optional minimum_revisions[shard_id]
Minima belong to this collection and fixed shard map. Wait or return not-ready without matches if any requested minimum is unmet; never claim read-your-delete on a degraded substitute.
collection-level measured recall and sample version
Per-segment statistics alone do not establish end-to-end recall.

blocks.text: This design fixes the shard map for a collection's lifetime; online repartitioning is not supported by this protocol. A writer locks the target shard counter, conditionally advances the vector's caller version and inserts the mutation in the same transaction. Only committed increments are visible; duplicate or stale writes allocate no new mutation. Return a collection-and-shard-qualified token, never a bare revision. Snapshot building reads raw vectors and all shard counters from the same consistent snapshot and stores the counter map in the manifest. Counter serialization is a capacity limit to benchmark; the map is not a global revision.

Pin each request to one manifest generation. A replica loads its shard's listed segments and raw snapshot, then replays that shard's revisions above snapshot_watermarks[shard_id] contiguously with per-vector version checks. The router combines write tokens by taking the maximum requested revision separately for each shard, and accepts only responses meeting every supplied minimum for this collection; replicas of other shards cannot satisfy it. Unmet minima yield not-ready without matches, not a degraded success. Publish only after whole-collection recall evaluation. Retain old artifacts and each shard's required history until pinned readers, rollback policy and replicas no longer need them; a missing range means remain unhealthy and reload a fresh snapshot.

blocks.title: Build, replay and visibility protocol
items: Authorise the collection and validate vector dimensions and distance convention. For cosine, explicitly normalise or use an engine’s cosine operator; never coerce an incompatible vector.

For broad filters, traverse nonmatching graph nodes when necessary but admit only matching current-version candidates. This is a serving-engine capability to implement or select, not a claim that every ANN library has the same filter semantics.
For selective filters, obtain the matching id set from a metadata index and exact-score it. Benchmark the crossover instead of assuming every small set is cheaper.
Query the mutable delta as well as pinned immutable segments. Suppress tombstoned and superseded versions before scoring candidates, then rerank raw vectors from the same snapshot-plus-delta state.
Scatter only to the collection’s shards. Hedge only within an explicit extra-work budget; return the number of healthy shard replies and mark a deadline-shortened response degraded.

Build raw vectors and the shard-counter map from the same consistent snapshot, write checked artifacts, run the collection's filtered and unfiltered recall suite, and conditionally publish the manifest with per-shard watermarks.
At swap, retain each shard's updates and tombstones above its own new snapshot watermark. Discard only mutations covered for that shard; old readers continue on their pinned generation.

Logical deletion becomes visible when its shard replica applies the tombstone. For read-your-delete, pass the returned token in minimum_revisions keyed by shard; the router requires that shard's watermark or returns not-ready without matches. Physical erasure from snapshots/backups has a separate retention policy.

blocks.text: Memory per vector is useful only when the index configuration and all overhead are specified. PQ shrinks codes, not graph links, metadata, replica copies or raw rerank data. Measure collection-level recall against exact search using representative filters and query vectors. A build can pass per-segment tests while failing the merged retrieval contract, so publication gates the whole serving configuration.

blocks.caption: Scaling controls.
rows: Pack isolated small collections carefully; add headroom and replica placement before choosing nodes.
Resident bytes, allocator overhead, delta and simultaneous old/new generations.
Hydrate raw snapshots to serving disks, batch candidate fetches, retain recent versions in delta.
Random IO and candidate count across all queried shards.
In-walk candidate filtering or exact scoring by selectivity.
Filtered recall, not just unfiltered benchmark score.
Separate builder pool with tenant quotas and capped database read bandwidth.
Shard revision counters with data; retain complete recovery history.
Lock contention, write amplification and catch-up duration.
Deadline and bounded hedges to a generation-matched replica.
Duplicate-work fraction and full-coverage query latency.

blocks.text: The original claim that a node serves thousands of queries with headroom was unmeasured. A hot collection can receive all peak traffic, and every shard of that collection then sees that traffic unless replicas split it. A node count inferred from memory is not a throughput plan. The same caution applies to managed OpenSearch: operational convenience does not establish this service’s filtered recall or latency.

blocks.caption: Failure and recovery.
rows: Replica handles traffic if warm and current
Replacement loads index plus raw snapshot, replays revisions, then becomes healthy.
Bounded hedge; deadline; explicit degraded and coverage fields.
No publication; retain prior generation and its recovery history.
Scale isolated build capacity; admission backpressure at hard delta cap.
Compact at measured ratio; logical filtering still applies before results.
Raw commit succeeds but dispatch fails
Pending intent dispatcher and independent revision polling recover; no write lost.
Remain unhealthy; obtain new consistent snapshot.
Reject before routing; never infer access from client filter values.
Default query may still show old version within freshness window
Minimum-revision queries wait or fail not-ready; physical erasure handled separately.

blocks.caption: Neutral memory-cost sensitivity, not a vendor quote or complete bill.
rows: Raw storage, metadata, headroom, IO, CPU, build overlap and operations

blocks.text: At larger scale, partition by a metadata key commonly present in queries only when it preserves the requested search scope; routing to fewer shards changes semantics if relevant neighbours live elsewhere. Quantisation and disk-resident graph engines are options, not mathematical necessities. Publish cost per configuration and let owners choose freshness tiers explicitly rather than silently weakening the existing target.

L1: An approximate nearest neighbour index (HNSW) behind a query API with metadata filtering and a stated recall target.
The raw size and index memory derived from the assumptions with the cited bytes-per-vector formula.
Upserts as delete plus insert with tombstones, and freshness through a delta.
L2: Sharding and replication of indexes with scatter-gather, hedged requests and a degraded flag for missed shards.
Build separated from serve, a whole-generation recall gate, watermark-preserving replay and pinned-generation rollback.
Quantisation with re-ranking against raw vectors, and the memory arithmetic that justifies it.
Filtered search by selectivity, with both failure modes of pre- and post-filtering explained.
L3: A multi-tenant vector platform: collections per large tenant, build and query quotas, a cost per million vectors per month per configuration.
Routing by a metadata partition key to avoid full scatter at a billion vectors, and disk-resident graphs for cold data.
When Postgres with a vector index is enough, and the rule for moving a collection to the service.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: approximate with measured recall, filter selectivity, upsert semantics, rebuilds without downtime, who owns the test set, whether a database is enough. Say the numbers aloud: 307 GB of raw vectors, 320 GB of HNSW memory at M equal to 16, 3.2 GB of PQ codes only at 32 bytes per vector, 5 arithmetic shard-equivalents replicated twice, before headroom and collection packing, 2,000 queries per second.

0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Collection with index parameters and a test set, Vector with version and metadata, Segment, Delta, Tombstones; the upsert, delete, query and rebuild endpoints with the recall tier.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: query router, shards with immutable segments and a delta, the change log, the segment builder, object storage, the raw store. Say why segments are immutable.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: memory and the build-versus-serve split (M, ef, quantisation, re-ranking, recall as a gate, rollback), then filtered search and isolation (in-walk versus exact scoring by selectivity, tenant as filter versus collection, hedging the tail).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (evaluate quantisation and disk-resident graphs per collection against recall gates, partition-key routing, quotas and cost per million vectors), and the L3 sentence: an index is a derived, disposable view with a measured recall; the design is about who builds it, when, and at what memory cost.

Context and scope: The products that need nearest-neighbour search, the collections and their sizes today, the database that holds the small ones, the latency or isolation problem that motivates a service.

Goals and non-goals: Recall at 10 of 0.95 measured, p99 of 50 ms unfiltered and 100 ms filtered, freshness within a minute, rebuilds without downtime, tenant isolation; no embedding computation, no text search, no hybrid ranking.
Design: This answer fills it: the serving and build paths, the segment model, the filtering strategy, the data model and API.
Alternatives considered: IVF or flat indexes, in-place mutation, a single filtering strategy, tenant-only sharding, a dedicated service for every collection, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security (per-tenant authentication and collection ownership), privacy (vectors can encode personal data; logical tombstones meet freshness; physical erasure from segments and backups has a separately stated retention bound), observability (recall per serving generation, p99 per shard, degraded ratio, delta age, tombstone ratio), cost (memory per vector per configuration, builder hours), rollout one collection at a time with the database path as fallback.
Review questions the doc must answer: How long after a delete the vector can still be returned, and what a caller receives when one shard misses the deadline.
